extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators / public speakers, rhetoricians, advocates, and students of classical rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and delivering public speeches (forum/forensic and deliberative oratory), covering invention, arrangement, style, delivery, and decorum. Focuses on how to select arguments, order them, and express them by voice, gesture, and language appropriate to audience and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atticism (correctness and elegance of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: To discourse plainly, and without any ornament, provided it be done correctly, and clearly, is the only genuine Atticism (as commonly supposed), but Atticism more broadly includes any expression that is perfectly correct, elegant, and free from fault or impertinence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid faulty, distasteful, or harsh expressions that would provoke ridicule (Aeschines ridiculing Demosthenes). Atticism does not mean only plainness: speakers like Lysias may be 'truly Attic' for having nothing faulty or impertinent; florid, nervous, and copious styles may still be Attic provided they are not faulty. Do not conflate Atticism with a single narrow mode of plainness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audience taste (decorum / to prepon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine what is becoming (to prepon) in language and sentiment — adapt style and sentiment to the rank, character, age, place, time, and hearers; not every subject or audience admits the same tone or expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what will be most 'becoming' in every part of an oration. Avoid lofty style for petty matters and avoid puerile subtlety when addressing grave crimes. Decorum governs both sentiment and turn of expression and prevents indecorum arising from topic, speaker, audience, or antagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of appropriate model/genre (distinguish orator from historian/poet/sophist/philosopher)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate oratorical language from that of historians (Thucydides), philosophers (Plato), poets, and Sophists; each genre has distinct purposes and aptitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not imitate styles unsuited to the Forum: Thucydides' obscure and intricate periods suit history, not public debate; Sophists and demonstrative oratory suit parade and schools rather than forensic pleading. Choose models (e.g., Lysias for simplicity, Demosthenes for force) appropriate to the intended public and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (mastery of sources of argument and proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be thoroughly acquainted with the sources of argument and proof: determine whether the point rests on fact, its legal denomination, or its agreement with justice; use common-places as sources for arguments and canvass a question on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey the 'common-places' fully, examine each argument's force, and select what is most pertinent. Beware fertile sources producing also many trivial or useless arguments — exercise judgment to pick, enlarge upon, or suppress as fits the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition / Arrangement (methodize and order arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodize what is to be said: make the entrance graceful and suitable; invalidate opposing matter early; present strongest arguments at the front and the close; introduce trifling arguments intermittently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the speech so the portal (opening) secures the hearer's goodwill. Weak arguments should be sprinkled where they help most; strongest arguments should appear at key positions (opening and conclusion) to maximize impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis and abstraction to general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract the point in debate from particular persons and times to a general thesis resting on universal principles, so that what is true universally applies to subordinate cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, move controversy from particulars to general topics (a thesis) to argue with more liberty and force. Employ Aristotle's common-places as marks for discovering arguments applicable on either side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and pruning of arguments (avoid 'weeds')
rubrics_metrics.description: From the plentiful common-places many arguments will arise, some trivial, foreign, or useless; the orator must carefully examine and select with propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and eliminate trivial or harmful material; enlarge upon pertinent points; soften or conceal harsh circumstances and, if necessary, divert attention to more favorable topics. Judgment in selection is essential to build a persuasive, focused case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold aims of Elocution: prove, delight, and force the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A finished orator 'can so speak, as to prove, delight, and force the passions.' Proving is necessary, delighting engages attention, and forcing the passions is often decisive in winning the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to aim: use neat and accurate diction chiefly for proving; a moderately florid style for delighting; and vehement, impetuous elocution for moving passions. A competent orator must temper and determine what is suitable in each part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and tempering of styles (adapt tempo, cadence, and ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different natures favor different manners: rapid torrent of words vs measured pauses; smooth equable periods vs harsh severe diction; nervous and majestic vs neat and simple — the orator must temper these varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many legitimate modes exist; exercise discretion to combine or shift modes according to subject and audience. Avoid monotony ('perpetual sameness' or 'tiresome uniformity'), and be able to employ rapidity, measured pauses, smoothness, or severity as the case requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elocution mechanics: voice modulation and pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Action and elocution include management of voice and gesture. The finished orator will employ a suitable and corresponding tone of voice; pronunciation bears principal sway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary pitch, volume, and speed to match sentiment: strong/quick voice for cutting material; mild/easy for calm; cool/settled for grave; plaintive/flexible for mournful. Practice and improve voice; pronunciation is of first importance (Demosthenes assigns primary place to pronunciation). Avoid artificial or whining modulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture, posture, and physical action
rubrics_metrics.description: Action is the eloquence of the body: proper management of voice, gesture, countenance, and eyes. Posture erect and manly; movements few, moderate, and purposeful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid superfluous or impertinent motions (effeminate airs, finical finger play, measured joint movements). Chief gesture: firm graceful sway of body, extend the arm when arguments press and draw back when vehemence abates. Advances should be few and not precipitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countenance and eyes as interpreters of the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The countenance is the image of the mind, the eyes its interpreters; their expression must be proportioned to the subject's importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the face is neither unmeaning nor ostentatious; leave much to the expression of the eyes. A well-managed countenance greatly enhances persuasion; awkward delivery of countenance can undo fine language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cadence, harmony, and periodic construction (rhyme/number) where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In demonstrative and ornamental species, employ harmonious sound, contrasts, antitheses, and 'number' (a prosaic metre or cadence) to please the ear and gratify attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such studied decorations suit panegyrics, essays, and the schools rather than the Forum. Use melodi­ous, well-turned periods and cadences to delight, but employ these ornaments sparingly in real pleadings to avoid seeming artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate imitation (anti-patterns: Thucydidean obscurity, Asiatic whining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain styles are inappropriate to public debate: Thucydides' obscure, intricate periods are unfit for the Forum; Asiatic 'whining sing-song' would be intolerable to Athenian ears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not copy historical or too-poetical styles that impair intelligibility in public speaking. Learn from models but avoid the extreme peculiarities that render speech obscure, puerile, or ridiculed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation: avoid excess and defect
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases every thing has its proper mean; an excess is always more offensive than a proportionable defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of over-ornamenting, over-velocity, overwrought gestures, or excessive simplicity. Discretion and moderation are the basis of eloquence; errors of excess offend more than modest deficiency.
